card: Deposits, staged payments and clear terms on every quote: how contractors stop chasing late payments before the job even starts.
title: How to Get Paid on Time as a Contractor
desc: How contractors get paid on time: taking deposits, staged progress payments, payment terms on every quote, and what to do when a client pays late.

blocks.h1: How to get paid on time: *set it up before the job starts.*
blocks.lede: Late payment is one of the most common money worries for contractors, and most of it is decided before the first tool comes out. Clear terms on the quote, a deposit, staged payments tied to stages of work and fast invoicing stop most problems before they start.
ticks: Terms to put on every quote
What to do when a client pays late

blocks.html:
How common is late payment?

Very. A 2026 industry survey reported that around 70% of contractors regularly get paid late. For a small business, one slow payer can mean covering wages and materials out of your own pocket.

Take a deposit

A deposit does three things: it covers materials, it confirms the customer is serious, and it means you are never fully out of pocket. Ask for it before you order materials or book the job in.

Check the rules where you work. Some places limit deposits on home improvement work. California, for example, caps them for many residential jobs. A quick check with your licensing body or trade association saves trouble later.

Use staged payments on bigger jobs

Split larger jobs into stages and tie each payment to a stage you can both see is finished:

StageExample payment
Booking and materialsDeposit
Demolition and prep finishedProgress payment 1
Main work finishedProgress payment 2
Handover and final checkFinal payment

You are never far ahead of what has been paid, and the customer only pays for work they can see.

Terms to put on every quote

  • The deposit amount and when it is due.
  • Each stage payment and what triggers it.
  • When the final invoice is due (for example, within 7 days of completion).
  • How they can pay: bank transfer, card or payment link.
  • What happens with variations: agreed in writing, priced before the work is done.
  • The expiry date of the quote.

Customers who agree to clear terms before the job starts rarely argue about them at the end.

Invoice the same day

Send the invoice the day each stage finishes, while the customer is happy with the work. Use invoicing software or a payment link so paying takes one tap. The longer you wait to invoice, the longer you wait to be paid.

When a client pays late

  1. Friendly reminder the day after it is due: “Just a reminder the invoice for your fence is due. Here is the link to pay.”
  2. Phone call a few days later. Often there is a simple reason you can sort out.
  3. Formal letter with a clear deadline, referring to the terms they agreed.
  4. Get advice. If it is still unpaid, speak to your trade association or a lawyer about your options where you work.

Attract better customers in the first place

Customers who find you because of your reviews and your work, rather than the cheapest price on a lead platform, are usually easier to work with and quicker to pay. A professional website with clear processes sets expectations before the first call. See what a trade website needs.

This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Example payment terms

Adapt something like this for your quotes (and check it suits the rules where you work):

“A deposit of [amount] is due to confirm your booking and before materials are ordered. Progress payments are due on completion of each stage listed above. The final invoice is due within 7 days of completion. Changes to the scope will be quoted in writing and agreed before the work is done. This quote is valid for 14 days.”

Why customers pay late

  • The invoice arrived weeks later and the job no longer feels urgent.
  • Paying is awkward: bank details buried in a PDF, no payment link.
  • There is a dispute about a variation that was never agreed in writing.
  • Cash flow problems on their side, especially with builders and commercial clients.

Most of these are fixed by invoicing the same day, offering easy payment and agreeing changes in writing.

Builders and commercial clients

Commercial work often comes with longer payment terms. Agree them before you start, invoice exactly as the contract asks, and keep copies of every approval. If a builder is often late, factor that into your price or limit how much work you take from them at once.

blocks.title: Your checklist.
items: Write standard payment terms for every quote
Take a deposit before ordering materials
Check local rules on deposit limits
Split big jobs into staged payments
Agree variations in writing before doing them
Invoice the same day each stage is finished
Offer a one tap payment link
Follow up late payments within a day

items.q: How much deposit should a contractor take?
items.a: It depends on the job and local rules. Many trades take enough to cover materials. Some places cap deposits on home improvement work, so check where you work.
Payments tied to stages of a job, such as preparation, main work and completion, so the customer pays as work is finished.

items.q: How do I ask a customer for payment politely?
items.a: Send a short reminder with a payment link the day after it is due, then call. Most late payers respond to a friendly, direct nudge.

items.q: Should I start work without a deposit?
items.a: It is risky, especially when you buy materials. A deposit confirms the customer is serious and protects your cash.

items.q: What should payment terms on a quote include?
items.a: The deposit, each stage payment and its trigger, when the final invoice is due, how to pay, how variations are handled and when the quote expires.
